entities.summary:
Angelus of Jerusalem, OCarm, was a Catholic convert from Judaism and a religious priest of the Carmelites of the Ancient Observance, active in the 13th century. 

Born around 1195 in Jerusalem, he later converted to Catholicism and was ordained as a priest. 

He was known for his missionary work and his efforts to convert Jews to Christianity, but his methods were often criticized by his contemporaries. 

Angelus of Jerusalem died on May 12, 1225, in Jerusalem, leaving behind a legacy of complex and often contentious religious beliefs.

The exact circumstances of his death are unknown, but it is believed that he may have been buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

His legacy is a testament to the complex and often fraught history of religious conversion and missionary work in the Middle East during the Middle Ages.

The conversion of a prominent Jewish figure to Christianity had significant implications for the relationships between Jews, Christians, and Muslims in the region, and continues to be a topic of debate and discussion among historians and scholars today.

In the centuries following his death, Angelus of Jerusalem was remembered as a key figure in the spread of Christianity in the Middle East, and his story has been retold and reinterpreted in various forms of art and literature.

Despite the controversy surrounding his methods, Angelus of Jerusalem remains an important figure in the history of religious conversion and missionary work, and his legacy continues to be felt in the complex and often fraught relationships between Jews, Christians, and Muslims in the region.
